findings.text: Within the first paragraph a newcomer can say what Athena is and how it differs from other tools (one model does the work, another checks it, and each step's cost is recorded). This is a strong opening.
findings.source: Athena is an open-source system, written in Rust, that turns a short request into a change to a code repository. It shows how it read the request, has one AI model do the work and a different one check it, and records what each step cost.

findings.text: This URL is Athena's home page, but the title and nearly all of the page are about a different project, firstmate. A newcomer who came to learn about Athena gets one paragraph on it, then about 40 claims about another tool's internals.

The page gives a reason for the study, and the cited claims with line-level source links back that reason up. But the page never says why that ability matters to the reader, and it never connects the study to Athena's main job of turning a request into a change.
findings.source: Athena made this study of firstmate to show that it can read an unfamiliar project and explain it with every statement traced to a claim, and every claim to lines in the project's own files.

findings.text: A clear next step is linked from the header, so a newcomer doesn't have to read the whole study to find out what to do.
findings.source: Next step: install Athena or read firstmate itself.

findings.text: The install steps leave gaps. There is no clone command, no prerequisites (a Rust toolchain? which AI models or API keys?), and no word on which repository `athena ask` acts on or what the reader will see afterwards.
findings.source: Next steps: "Install Athena from a checkout of its repository: ./setup.sh" / "Try it with a one-line request: athena ask "add a changelog""

findings.text: Elsewhere the page uses "place" to mean a worker slot (glossary entry "place": "One of a project's worker slots"). Using the same word for a home is confusing in a page whose counter is called places-held.
findings.source: Words used first, home: "A firstmate home is the place that holds a backlog of tasks."

findings.text: Several terms a newcomer meets are never defined: "unheld", "wake" (the glossary's "stale wake" is "A wake after which…"), "endpoint", "captain-held inventory", "harness pin" and "crewmates".
findings.source: One piece of work, start to finish: "A spawn is accepted only for an unheld, unblocked item."

findings.text: The ordering means the reader hits "green" before the term it depends on. The page is honest that it doesn't know what "in scope" means, but that leaves the yolo rule only half explained.
findings.source: Words used first: "green — A PR that is not red" appears before "red" is defined; "in scope … this page gives no test for it."

findings.text: The step-by-step walkthrough is the easiest part of the firstmate study to follow. Each step is short, and each step's citation links to the claim behind it.
findings.source: One piece of work, start to finish (ordered list, steps 1–8)

findings.text: The limits section uses Athena-internal wording ("job", "recorded boundary", "edge") that a stranger can't decode. The plain point, that firstmate was read but never run, is buried.
findings.source: Limits of this study, f1: "The job gave no recorded boundary for running firstmate, so no failure or retry edge was observed"

findings.text: The page doesn't say which repository holds this `studies/` folder, so a newcomer can't find the source data without guessing.
findings.source: About this page: "the name of the folder under studies/ that holds the data this page is generated from."
